name: Nikhil Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I haul shipping containers out of the port for a logistics contractor, mostly to the big inland depots about two hours away. I queue at the port gate, get a container dropped onto my trailer by the crane, check the seal and the paperwork, then drive it out and do it again. I like the scale of it, the ships, the cranes, all of it moving. What wears me out is the queues at the gate, sometimes ninety minutes of sitting there, and backing a forty-foot trailer into a tight depot slot, which I still mess up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does tech come into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, for me. I use an AI assistant to check customs codes, plan fuel stops, and I've been using it to learn about investing during the gate queues. I've got about a year of money saved and some in index funds. I share a flat with my brother Kenji, who works in software, so we argue about AI over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit surprised, but fine, the tools are still useful. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype cycle got ahead of the tech. At the port nobody would care, they'd just complain about the gate queues as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep doing this and building money. Port haulage pays well, and there's always work because ships keep coming. My only worries are getting better at reversing and not burning out on the long hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep putting money into the index funds, maybe five hundred a month. I'd use the AI to keep learning things in the queues, like the customs side, because that's useful whatever happens. I might look at a side project, like a small app for drivers to share gate queue times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the gate queue app.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every driver in the gate queue is on their phone anyway, so why not share how long the line is? I built a rough version with the AI's help, it's just a group chat with a bot in it. If it caught on, maybe the port would pay for something proper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your brother say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji would be relieved, honestly, he's always half worried AI will write his code. He'd say the plateau is the best of both worlds. I'd say the same for me.

say: I'd say the **hype cycle** got ahead of the tech, but the tools are **still useful**.
At the port, people would just complain about **gate queues** as usual.
think: Port haulage pays well and there's **always work** because ships keep coming.
My worries are **reversing** and **burning out** on long hours.
do: Put about **five hundred** a month into index funds.
Use **AI** in the queues to learn the **customs** side.
Build a small **gate queue** app for drivers.
S0.quote: Every driver in the gate queue is on their phone anyway, so why not share how long the line is?
fieldNote: He treats **idle queue time** as learning and building time.
He's already **investing** and thinking about a side project.
His brother's **software job** gives him a second view on AI at home.

steps.text: Put about five hundred a month into index funds
Learn customs codes with his AI assistant during gate queues
Turn his gate-queue chat bot into a small paid app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is actually good if you're willing to learn. Online I'd post that drivers should get on the tools now, not wait. At the port I'd show people how I check customs codes in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's fine for me for a few years. The paperwork side gets easier, the booking side gets automated, and my driving stays. The port is already testing self-driving carriers inside the terminal, so I know robots are coming, just slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the new booking systems the day they appear and try to be the go-to driver for them. I'd keep investing, and I'd start looking at the port's automation team, the people who look after the self-driving carriers. Maybe a technician course, evenings, in the second half of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said self-driving carriers inside the terminal. What have you seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a section of the port where the machines that move containers between the cranes and the stacks run on their own. They go slowly and on fixed routes, but they work. The people who keep the self-driving port machines running are a safer bet than drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the contractor would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners who match drivers to containers, definitely. There's a guy called Dmitri who does it all on the phone and a spreadsheet. If AI does that, he's the one who loses out, not me.

say: I'd say this is **good** if you're willing to learn.
I'd urge drivers to get on the **tools now**, not wait.
think: My driving stays for a few years while **paperwork and booking** get automated.
The port is already **testing self-driving** carriers, so robots are coming slowly.
do: Adopt new **booking systems** the day they arrive.
Start an evening **technician course** later in the year.
S1.quote: The people who keep the self-driving port machines running are a safer bet than drivers.
fieldNote: He has **seen automation** at work in the terminal and draws a clear lesson.
He'd aim to be the **go-to driver** for new systems.
He names the **planner** as the one most exposed, not himself.

steps.text: Use the new container booking system from its first day
Start an evening technician course in the second half of the year
Keep investing about five hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shift and everyone needs to move fast, including governments. Online I'd be sharing what I'm learning so other drivers can keep up. At the port I'd say don't waste a single month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me. My thinking side is small, so 2028 doesn't hit me much, but around 2031 the trucks drive themselves, and port to depot is a simple, repeated route. Even the technician jobs I fancied might be done by robots soon after, so there's no safe corner to hide in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get onto a technician course straight away and try to get hired by the port's automation team before everyone else tries. I'd move some of my savings into shares in automation and robot companies, so if my job goes, at least my money grows. I'd keep the flat with Kenji to keep costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but my brain would be going all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking work changes in 2028 and the driving about 2031. What do you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat those three years as a countdown. Learn the technical side, get my foot in the door at the automation team, and stack as much money as I can. By 2031 I want to be on the other side of the robot, not in its seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kenji? His work is more thinking work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the funny part, he'd go first in this one. He'd be out in 2028 and I'd still be driving. We'd probably end up pooling money, and I'd be the one paying the rent for a while.

say: I'd say everyone, **governments** included, must move **fast**.
I'd share what I'm learning so **other drivers** can keep up.
think: Port to depot is a **simple route**, so driving goes around **2031**.
Even **technician jobs** might fall to robots, leaving no safe corner.
do: Apply to the port's **automation team** before others do.
S2.quote: By 2031 I want to be on the other side of the robot, not in its seat.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a countdown to use, not a reprieve.
His **brother** loses out first here, flipping who supports whom.
Buying **robot shares** is a deliberate hedge against his own job.

steps.text: Enrol on a technician course in the first month
Apply to the port's automation team before 2029
Move part of his savings into automation company shares
Pool money with his brother to cover the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to learn. I'd be a bit preachy online, telling drivers to use the time. At work I'd be the one showing people how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's okay. The robots come around 2034, and by then I'd have a technician qualification and a few years in the automation side. The thinking side in 2031 barely touches what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for two years, put serious money into investments, and do the technician course part time. In year three, I'd try to move into the automation team. I'd keep building the gate queue app on the side, maybe even sell it to the port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The automation team might stay tiny, maybe five jobs for the whole port. Then it's me against everyone else with the same idea. So I'd want a second option, like moving into the companies that build the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel driving the last few years, knowing what's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, but fine. I'd treat my last years of driving like the last year of school, enjoy it, take the money, and leave on my own terms. I'd rather leave than be pushed.

say: I'd say **five years** is plenty for anyone willing to **learn**.
I'd be the one showing coworkers how to use the **tools**.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'd have a **technician** qualification.
The thinking changes in 2031 **barely touch** my driving work.
do: Drive for **two more years** while investing seriously.
Do the **technician course** part time and join the automation team in year three.
Keep building the **gate queue app** and pitch it to the port.
S3.quote: I'd treat my last years of driving like the last year of school, enjoy it, take the money, and leave on my own terms.
fieldNote: He sees the **automation team** may be too small and plans a second option.
He wants to leave on his **own terms**, not be pushed.
His **side app** becomes a possible exit route.

steps.text: Invest a large share of his pay for two years
Take the technician course part time
Move into the port automation team in year three
Pitch the gate-queue app to the port authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real opportunity, so people shouldn't treat it as a threat. Online I'd be the optimistic one. I'd tell the younger drivers to pick a direction in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm well placed. I'd be thirty-nine in 2039, and I'd have had ten years of good pay, investing, and learning. I don't see myself driving by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for a few years and keep investing. I'd move into the technical side around 2030, and maybe build something of my own with Kenji, like a small software tool for logistics firms. I'd take my time and choose well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about the ten years a risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. If I'm on good money and nothing's changing yet, it's easy to just keep driving. I'd set myself checkpoints, every year, to see if I'm still on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning building something with Kenji. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that helps small haulage firms keep up, like booking and gate times in one simple app. My brother does the code, and I know what drivers actually need. It's a long shot, but a decade is long enough to try.

say: I'd say **ten years** is an **opportunity**, not a threat.
I'd tell younger drivers to **pick a direction** within two years.
think: I'm **well placed**, with a decade of pay, **investing** and learning.
I don't see myself **driving** by 2039 anyway.
do: Keep driving and **investing** for a few years.
Build a **logistics app** for small haulage firms with my brother.
S4.quote: My brother does the code, and I know what drivers actually need.
fieldNote: His main risk, in his own words, is **getting comfortable**.
He'd set **yearly checkpoints** to keep himself honest.
A **joint venture** with his brother is his long-term bet.

steps.text: Keep investing monthly in index funds
Move into the port's technical side around 2030
Build a booking and gate-time app with his brother

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because port driving is easy to automate and three years isn't much time to get into the technical side. What would help is the port and the contractor offering real technician training to drivers, and paying us while we learn, instead of hiring outsiders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the gate queues, and I'm only half joking. If AI could fix the ninety-minute wait at the port gate, drivers would love it overnight.

headlineQuote: If AI could fix the ninety-minute wait at the port gate, drivers would love it overnight.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** container haulier at a port, still shaky at **reversing** forty-foot trailers.
He uses **AI daily**, invests regularly, and has about a year of savings.
He has watched **self-driving** machines in the terminal and plans to move into the automation side.
He sees **port-to-depot** driving as highly exposed and treats any warning time as a countdown.
He stays **calm** in most pictures, becoming **anxious** only in the fastest one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving little time to move into **technical** work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid technician training** for drivers from the port and the contractor.
